import { Canvas, Controls, Description, Meta, Primary, Title } from "@storybook/addon-docs/blocks";

import { DesignTokensTable } from "#storybook/_components/DesignTokensTable/DesignTokensTable";
import tokens from "#tokens/components/ams/button.tokens.json";

import * as ButtonStories from "./Button.stories.tsx";

<Meta of={ButtonStories} />

<Title />

<Description of={ButtonStories} />

<Primary />

<Controls />

## Usage guidelines

### When to use

Use a Button to start an action, submit a form, or change the state of the interface.

### When not to use

Don’t use a Button to navigate to another page.
Use a [Standalone Link](/docs/components-navigation-standalone-link--docs) or a [Call to Action Link](/docs/components-navigation-call-to-action-link--docs) instead, or an inline [Link](/docs/components-navigation-link--docs) in running text.

### How to use

Use only one primary Button per screen.
The primary variant draws attention to the most important action; multiple primaries dilute that signal.

Set `type="submit"` to make the Button submit the surrounding form.

Wrap two or more Buttons or links that sit next to each other in an [Action Group](/docs/components-layout-action-group--docs).

Always provide a short, descriptive label that names the action.
For icon-only Buttons, supply the label through the `children` prop – it is read by screen readers even though it is not shown.

### How to write

Write a short label that names the action.
Use the verb's infinitive form in Dutch, e.g. 'Verwijderen' or 'Opslaan', not 'Verwijder' or 'Sla op'.
Avoid generic labels like 'Klik hier' or 'OK'.

## Examples

### Primary

A primary Button draws attention to the most important call to action.

<Canvas of={ButtonStories.Primary} />

### Secondary

Use a secondary Button for other actions.

<Canvas of={ButtonStories.Secondary} />

### Tertiary

Tertiary Buttons distinguish themselves from secondary Buttons when even less emphasis is needed.
They are also the choice for icon-only Buttons.

<Canvas of={ButtonStories.Tertiary} />

### Disabled

A disabled Button gets a grey background in every variant.
The primary variant uses a darker grey than the secondary and tertiary ones, because its label is white.
Switch off `disabled` to compare the three with their normal appearance.

<Canvas of={ButtonStories.Disabled} />

### With icon

Add an icon if it makes the Button’s purpose easier or faster to recognise.
The icon appears after the label by default.

<Canvas of={ButtonStories.WithIcon} />

### With icon before

The icon can also appear before the label.

<Canvas of={ButtonStories.WithIconBefore} />

### With icon only

A Button can consist of just an icon, but only one of our [functional icons](/docs/brand-assets-icons--docs#functional-icons).
You must still provide a label for screen reader users.
If the icon-only Button must align with surrounding text, use an [Icon Button](/docs/components-buttons-icon-button--docs) instead.

<Canvas of={ButtonStories.WithIconOnly} />

### Text wrapping

The label may wrap over multiple lines when no shorter text is available, when two Buttons sit next to each other on a narrow screen, or when the user has configured a large font on their device.

<Canvas of={ButtonStories.TextWrapping} />

## Features

The Button handles its own focus, hover, active, and disabled states.
On narrow screens or with longer labels, it wraps text without losing alignment.

## Design

The three variants form a hierarchy of importance: primary, secondary, tertiary.
This lets a screen present one clear focal action without ranking every other Button against it.

A label is set at the same size and weight as body text, with a tighter line height of 1.4 against the 1.6 of running text.
Nothing about the type marks a Button as important; its colour and its filled shape do that.

All three variants carry a border of the same width, and the corners are square.
A tertiary Button keeps that border transparent until the pointer is over it, and a secondary Button thickens its outline with an inset shadow rather than a wider border.
Neither changes the space a Button takes up, so a row of Buttons never shifts as one of them is hovered.

Hover styling applies only where a pointer can actually hover.
On a touch screen it would otherwise stay behind after a tap, leaving the Button that was pressed last looking active.

The button overrides the icon’s line height with its own, so the icon sits on the label’s line rather than on a taller one of its own.
The icon keeps its default size, the same body-text size the label uses.
An icon-only Button is square: the icon is given a square box, and the padding is equal on all four sides.

A label that does not fit is hyphenated rather than left to overflow.
The browser decides where to split it, so the [language of the document](/docs/docs-developer-guide-localisation--docs#specify-the-language-for-the-entire-document) must be set correctly.

In print, a Button keeps its background and border colours instead of being flattened to save ink.

## Accessibility

A Button renders a `button` element, which brings keyboard focus, activation with both Enter and Space, and the `button` role with it.

Its `type` defaults to `button` rather than to `submit`.
A Button inside a form therefore leaves that form alone until asked otherwise, which is why submitting takes an explicit `type="submit"`.

An icon-only Button takes its accessible name from the `children` you pass.
That text is rendered in the markup and hidden visually, so screen readers announce the same words a visible label would have carried, and the icon adds nothing to the name.

Disabling a Button with the `disabled` attribute removes it from the tab order, so a keyboard user never lands on it and reads no reason for it being unavailable.
The same appearance applies to `aria-disabled="true"`, which keeps the Button focusable and lets assistive technology announce it as disabled.

## See also

- [Icon Button](/docs/components-buttons-icon-button--docs) – an icon-only button aligned with surrounding text.
- [Standalone Link](/docs/components-navigation-standalone-link--docs) – for navigation to another page.
- [Call to Action Link](/docs/components-navigation-call-to-action-link--docs) – a prominent link styled like a Button.
- [Action Group](/docs/components-layout-action-group--docs) – lays out multiple Buttons and links.
- [Prose](/docs/utilities-css-prose--docs) – applies the recommended vertical spacing for editorial content.

import { Canvas, Controls, Description, Meta, Primary, Title } from "@storybook/addon-docs/blocks";

import * as IconButtonStories from "./IconButton.stories.tsx";

<Meta of={IconButtonStories} />

<Title />

<Description of={IconButtonStories} />

<Primary />

<Controls />

## Usage guidelines

### When to use

Choose an Icon Button instead of a regular Button when it must align with text.
Match the size of the Icon Button to the surrounding text.

### When not to use

Only [functional icons](/docs/brand-assets-icons--docs#functional-icons) belong in an Icon Button.
For other icons, use a [Button](/docs/components-buttons-button--docs) so that the user can read its label.

Do not use an Icon Button to submit a form; that is a [Button](/docs/components-buttons-button--docs)’s job.
Even the one icon-only submit in the system — the search button — is a Button, not an Icon Button.

### How to use

An Icon Button still needs a label for screen reader users.
Provide it through the `label` prop; it is read aloud even though it is not shown.

## Examples

### On a coloured background

An Icon Button on a coloured background must set [the correct text colour](/docs/brand-design-tokens-colour--docs#pairing-foreground-with-background-colours) to provide enough contrast.
We have light and dark background colours, and Icon Buttons behave differently on each.

#### Contrast colour

Use the contrast colour on a lime, orange or yellow background.
It will make the icon black.

<Canvas of={IconButtonStories.ContrastColour} />

#### Inverse colour

Use the inverse colour on an azure, blue, green, magenta or purple background.
It will make the icon white.

<Canvas of={IconButtonStories.InverseColour} />

## Design

An Icon Button has no shape of its own: no border, no background, and no padding.
It takes up no more room than the icon it holds, which is what lets it sit inside a line of text without disturbing the line.

The icon is given a square box, so the area that responds to the pointer is a square centred on the icon rather than a shape that follows its outline.
Hovering tints that square with the icon’s own colour at one-eighth opacity instead of filling it, so the affordance appears without the icon shifting or changing weight.

The focus outline is offset from the icon rather than drawn against it, which keeps a thin glyph readable inside the ring.

## Accessibility

An Icon Button renders a `button` element and always writes its label into the markup, hidden visually.
Screen readers announce that label, so the button is never announced as unlabelled, and the icon contributes nothing to the name.

Its `type` defaults to `button` rather than `submit`, so it never submits a form by accident: a close button dismisses a Dialog through its click handler, not by submitting a form the Dialog may contain.

## See also

- [Button](/docs/components-buttons-button--docs) – for actions that show a text label.
- [Icon](/docs/components-media-icon--docs) – a non-interactive icon.

import { Canvas, Controls, Description, Meta, Primary, Title } from "@storybook/addon-docs/blocks";

import { DesignTokensTable } from "#storybook/_components/DesignTokensTable/DesignTokensTable";
import tokens from "#tokens/components/ams/accordion.tokens.json";

import * as AccordionStories from "./Accordion.stories.tsx";
import * as AccordionSectionStories from "./AccordionSection.stories.tsx";

<Meta of={AccordionStories} />

<Title />

<Description of={AccordionStories} />

<Primary />

<Controls />

## Subcomponents

### Section

Pairs a heading with collapsible content.
Use `defaultExpanded` to show the content initially.
Pass `onToggle` to be notified when the section opens or closes.

<Canvas of={AccordionSectionStories.Section} />

<Controls of={AccordionSectionStories.Section} />

## Usage guidelines

### When to use

Use an Accordion to keep secondary content collapsed by default, so the primary content of a page stays prominent.
A typical example is a list of frequently asked questions.

### When not to use

Don’t hide essential information in an Accordion.
Users may not realise it is there.

For long content that deserves its own page, split it across multiple pages instead.
That often improves both usability and findability through search engines.

### How to use

Use between 3 and 10 sections.
Fewer is rarely worth the extra interaction; more makes the list hard to scan.

Provide each section with a clear, descriptive label.
Users cannot scan the content inside a collapsed section.

Set `headingLevel` on the Accordion to match its position in the page hierarchy.
All sections share that level.

### How to write

Write labels that describe what the user will find inside the section.
Use sentence case.

## Examples

### Expanded by default

Pass `defaultExpanded` to a section to make it visible from the start.
Use this sparingly – it works against the goal of keeping content collapsed.

<Canvas of={AccordionStories.ExpandedByDefault} />

### Reduce landmarks

An Accordion Section renders a `<section>` element by default, which creates a landmark region.
Many landmarks on one page can be noisy for screen reader users.
For Accordions with six or more sections, render generic `<div>` elements through `sectionAs="div"`.

<Canvas of={AccordionStories.ReduceLandmarks} />

## Features

The Accordion provides the heading and the show-or-hide behaviour.
Section content can include formatted text, links, and other components.

### Keyboard navigation

| Key             | Behaviour                                                 |
| :-------------- | :-------------------------------------------------------- |
| Enter or Space  | Open or close the focused section                         |
| Tab / Shift+Tab | Move to the next or previous focusable element            |
| Down / Up arrow | Move focus to the next or previous section (wraps around) |
| Home / End      | Move focus to the first or last section                   |

### Find in page

Browser ‘Find in page’ (Ctrl+F or ⌘+F) does not search inside collapsed sections.
If you can anticipate the search term, expand the relevant section automatically.

## Design

Section headings stay visible while their content collapses.
This lets users scan every section label without expanding anything.

Opening one section does not close the others.
A user looking for a specific answer can leave related context open as they explore.

The control is the heading rather than a button beside it.
The button fills the width of the heading and takes its typeface, size, weight and line height, so the thing that looks like a heading is the thing you click, all the way to the end of the line.

Its label starts where the surrounding text starts: there is no indent, and the chevron sits before the label rather than pushing it inward.
An Accordion therefore lines up with the content above and below it instead of forming a box of its own.

Sections are separated by white space alone, without rules or panels.
The chevron and the heading carry the affordance, which keeps a long list of sections from reading as a stack of boxes.

The chevron turns half a circle when a section opens.
It is animated only for users who have not asked for reduced motion; everyone else sees it arrive already turned.

## Accessibility

Each section renders a heading containing a button that reports whether it is expanded and names the panel it controls.
Screen readers therefore reach the sections by heading, as they would any other outline, and hear the state of each one.

A collapsed panel is removed from the page rather than hidden visually, so its content is not announced, not reachable by keyboard, and — as ‘Find in page’ above explains — not searchable.

The panel is a `section` labelled by its own heading, which makes it a landmark.
This is the reason ‘Reduce landmarks’ offers `sectionAs="div"`: six or more sections put six or more regions in the landmark list, and a landmark per collapsed paragraph tells a screen reader user less than it costs them to walk past.

## See also

- [Prose](/docs/utilities-css-prose--docs) – applies the recommended vertical spacing for editorial content.

import { Canvas, Controls, Description, Meta, Primary, Title } from "@storybook/addon-docs/blocks";

import { DesignTokensTable } from "#storybook/_components/DesignTokensTable/DesignTokensTable";
import tokens from "#tokens/components/ams/dialog.tokens.json";

import * as DialogStories from "./Dialog.stories.tsx";

<Meta of={DialogStories} />

<Title />

<Description of={DialogStories} />

<Primary />

<Controls />

## Usage guidelines

### When to use

Use a Dialog for short and non-frequent tasks.

### When not to use

Use Dialogs sparingly because they interrupt the user’s workflow.
Consider using the main flow for regular tasks.

### How to use

To open the Dialog, use `Dialog.open(dialogId)` from the React package.
To close it, either call the `Dialog.close` function or add a `<form>` as in the ‘confirmation’ example.

Wrap multiple buttons in an [Action Group](/docs/components-layout-action-group--docs).

#### Focusing a specific element

When a Dialog opens (and no element has `autofocus`), the browser places focus on the first focusable element inside it.
In this component that is the close button, which is a safe default: the user can read the Dialog before acting.

To give another element the initial focus instead, add the `autofocus` attribute to it, or the `autoFocus` prop in React.
Use this for the single element you expect the user to act on first, such as a text field or the primary Button.

Moving the initial focus has risks, so choose that element with care:

- Focus that lands past the heading and body text can cause screen reader users to skip the explanation above it. Only move focus when one element clearly comes first.
- Don’t place focus on a destructive or irreversible action. A user confirming by reflex with Enter or Space could lose data. In the confirmation example below, focus the option that keeps the user’s data safe.
- On touchscreen devices, autofocus on a text field opens the on-screen keyboard immediately, which can hide part of the Dialog.

For more information: [MDN: the dialog element](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/dialog#accessibility).

## Examples

### Asking to confirm

Use a `form` when asking the user to confirm an action, e.g. through ‘OK’ and ‘Cancel’ buttons.
Add `method="dialog"` to make the browser close the Dialog when the form is submitted.
Wrap multiple Buttons in an [Action Group](/docs/components-layout-action-group--docs) and place it in the `footer`.
Add an `id` to the form and use it in the `form` attribute of the buttons.
Set a `value` on each button to identify which one was clicked.
Consult [MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element/dialog#handling_the_return_value_from_the_dialog) for more information.

<Canvas of={DialogStories.Confirmation} />

## Features

The Dialog is a [query container](/docs/utilities-css-query-container--docs) for inline size, so elements inside it can adapt their appearance to the width of the Dialog.

### Keyboard navigation

| Key         | Behaviour                                                        |
| :---------- | :--------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Tab         | Moves focus to the next focusable element inside the Dialog.     |
| Shift + Tab | Moves focus to the previous focusable element inside the Dialog. |
| Arrow keys  | Scroll the body when it has focus and its content overflows.     |
| Escape      | Closes the Dialog.                                               |

## Design

A Dialog is built from three bands: a header with the heading and the close button, a body, and an optional footer.
Only the body scrolls.
The heading stays readable and the actions stay reachable however long the content grows, which is what keeps a user from scrolling to find the button they were looking for.

Scrolling inside the body does not continue into the page behind once it reaches the end.
Space for the scrollbar is reserved whether or not one appears, so the text does not shift sideways as content loads.

Its width and its maximum height both change at the medium breakpoint, and a maximum width caps it beyond that.
A Dialog is sized against the window rather than against its content, so it opens at a predictable size instead of filling the screen when it happens to hold a lot.

The three bands are told apart by their padding alone; nothing is drawn between them.
In forced colours mode that is not enough, so the header and the footer gain hairline separators there, marking the edges of the part that scrolls.

Forced colours also draws the border in the system colour and gives it a floor of one pixel, so a theme that sets the border token to zero cannot leave the Dialog without an edge against the page behind it.

## Accessibility

A Dialog renders the native `dialog` element and is opened as a modal.
The browser then makes the rest of the page inert, keeps Tab inside the Dialog without any focus trap of our own, closes it on Escape, and returns focus to whatever opened it.

The heading is a level 1 Heading shown at the size of a level 3.
A Dialog is its own document as far as its content is concerned, so the outline inside it starts afresh rather than continuing the page underneath.

The body takes keyboard focus in its own right, so someone navigating by keyboard can scroll long content with the arrow keys even when nothing inside it is focusable, as [WCAG 2.1.1](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#keyboard) requires.
Chromium and Firefox already make an overflowing scroll container focusable; Safari does not, so the Dialog makes the body focusable itself.

Scrolling of the page behind the Dialog is suppressed while it is open, but only where the browser supports the selector this relies on.
Opening a modal does not lock scrolling on its own, and iOS Safari still needs JavaScript for a guarantee, so a gesture over the backdrop there can move the page underneath.

## See also

- [Action Group](/docs/components-layout-action-group--docs) – lays out multiple Buttons.

import { Canvas, Controls, Description, Meta, Primary, Title } from "@storybook/addon-docs/blocks";

import { DesignTokensTable } from "#storybook/_components/DesignTokensTable/DesignTokensTable";
import tokens from "#tokens/components/ams/page.tokens.json";

import * as PageStories from "./Page.stories.tsx";

<Meta of={PageStories} />

<Title />

<Description of={PageStories} />

<Primary />

<Controls />

## Usage guidelines

### When to use

The Page component wraps the [Page Header](/docs/components-containers-page-header--docs), [Page Footer](/docs/components-containers-page-footer--docs), and the main content in between.
As a root layout component, it must be used for all websites for the City of Amsterdam.

### How to use

#### Public websites

Use the Page as it is.
Its children – a [Skip Link](/docs/components-navigation-skip-link--docs), the Page Header, the sections of the page, and the Page Footer – follow one another in document order.
See [Page structure](/docs/pages-guidelines-page-structure--docs) for the structure of a page.

#### Internal websites

Set `withMenu` to lay the Page out as a grid, with a column for the [Menu](/docs/components-navigation-menu--docs) beside the header, the body, and the footer.
Every child then needs the class name of the area it belongs in, such as `ams-page__area--header`.
The description of `withMenu` in the table above names all five.

Those rules apply to direct children of the Page only, so none of these elements may be wrapped in another one.
See the [introduction to the internal templates](/docs/pages-internal-introduction--docs) for the structure of a page.

## Examples

### Public websites

Navigation sits in the Page Header, so no Menu is involved.
See the [Home Page](/story/pages-public-home-page--default) template for a full-page example.

### Internal websites

Internal websites can add a [Menu](/docs/components-navigation-menu--docs) for navigating between its modules and pages.
This is an alternative to the approach using Link Lists, which is appropriate for public, content-oriented websites.

We can’t display the example here, as it requires Compact Mode to be enabled, which affects the example for the public Home Page template.
Open the [full example page](/story/components-containers-page--with-menu) or see the [Home Page](/story/pages-internal-home-page--default) template.

## Features

The Page is a [query container](/docs/utilities-css-query-container--docs) for inline size, so elements inside it can adapt their appearance to the width of the page.
For elements inside a [Grid Cell](/docs/components-layout-grid--docs) or [Dialog](/docs/components-containers-dialog--docs), that nearer container takes precedence; the Page covers everything else.

## Design

The Page is centered horizontally and sets a maximum width of 90 rems (usually 1440 pixels).
With a Menu, that becomes 120 rems (1920 pixels).

An element placed directly in the Page, outside a [Grid](/docs/components-layout-grid--docs), spans the full width of the Page rather than the full width of the window.

The Page is at least as tall as the window, measured against the part of it that is actually visible rather than the nominal height.
On a phone the browser’s own bars come and go as you scroll, and the two measurements differ by exactly that much; using the visible one keeps a short page from ending in a strip of background below the Page Footer.

With a Menu the Page becomes a grid of named areas rather than a stack.
The Skip Link keeps a row of its own across the full width, above both the menu column and the header, so it is still the first thing reached however the rest is arranged.

## Accessibility

A Page renders a `div` and adds nothing to the accessibility tree.
The landmarks of a page come from what you put inside it: the `banner` of the [Page Header](/docs/components-containers-page-header--docs), the `contentinfo` of the [Page Footer](/docs/components-containers-page-footer--docs), and the `main` element around the content between them.

With a Menu, the areas are placed by the grid rather than by their order in the markup.
The children are still announced and reached by keyboard in the order they are written, which is why the Skip Link comes first in the code as well as on screen.

## See also

- [Skip Link](/docs/components-navigation-skip-link--docs) – the first element in the Page, above the Page Header.
- [Page Header](/docs/components-containers-page-header--docs) – sits at the top of the Page.
- [Menu](/docs/components-navigation-menu--docs) – fills the menu column that `withMenu` adds, on an internal website.
- [Page Footer](/docs/components-containers-page-footer--docs) – sits at the bottom of the Page.

## Design tokens

<DesignTokensTable tokens={tokens} />

import { Canvas, Controls, Description, Meta, Primary, Title } from "@storybook/addon-docs/blocks";

import { DesignTokensTable } from "#storybook/_components/DesignTokensTable/DesignTokensTable";
import tokens from "#tokens/components/ams/page-footer.tokens.json";

import * as PageFooterStories from "./PageFooter.stories.tsx";
import * as PageFooterMenuStories from "./PageFooterMenu.stories.tsx";
import * as PageFooterMenuLinkStories from "./PageFooterMenuLink.stories.tsx";

<Meta of={PageFooterStories} />

<Title />

<Description of={PageFooterStories} />

<Primary />

This component has no props to configure.

## Subcomponents

The Spotlight subcomponent provides the blue area at the top of the Page Footer.
It has no props of its own; the example above shows it in place.

### Menu

Presents the links in the Spotlight.
Its visually hidden `heading` describes the menu for users of assistive technology.

<Canvas of={PageFooterMenuStories.Menu} />

<Controls of={PageFooterMenuStories.Menu} />

### Menu Link

Navigates to a page.
Set `linkComponent` to integrate with a routing library.

<Canvas of={PageFooterMenuLinkStories.MenuLink} />

<Controls of={PageFooterMenuLinkStories.MenuLink} />

## Usage guidelines

### When to use

The Page Footer must be used on all websites for the City of Amsterdam.
It must be the same on every page of the website.

### How to use

The content section is required for public websites, but not for internal ones.
It offers space for various practical links:

- The first column focuses on contact information.
  Make it specific and tailor it to the website or page.
- The second column contains links to other relevant sources.
- The third column refers to newsletters, events, social media, etc.

The menu is for links to privacy policies, cookie statements, and other information about the website itself.

Set [the inverse colour](/docs/brand-design-tokens-colour--docs#pairing-foreground-with-background-colours) on all text and links in this area.

If the Page Footer contains [Headings](/docs/components-text-heading--docs), give them level 2 and a size of 'level-3'.
A visually hidden heading to group them is not necessary – the footer's landmark provides enough guidance.

The menu includes a visually hidden heading for screen reader users.
The default heading text is 'Over deze website'.
Customize it when the menu serves a different purpose, or the interface language is not Dutch.

## Examples

### Custom content

The Page Footer for a specific website can be a bit different.
Here’s an example for the ‘Onderzoek en Statistiek’ department.

<Canvas of={PageFooterStories.CustomContent} />

### Custom menu heading

For an English website, update the visually hidden heading to ‘Support links’.
If your website is in Dutch, but the default heading of ‘Over deze website’ doesn’t reflect the content of the menu, choose a different heading as well.

<Canvas of={PageFooterStories.CustomMenuHeading} />

## Design

The Page Footer is two bands: a blue Spotlight holding the content, and a white strip below it holding the menu.
The change of colour is what separates them, so neither band needs a rule or a border to mark where it ends.

The menu links wrap onto as many lines as they need, with a wide gap between links and a narrow one between lines.
Links stay grouped by row that way, instead of the rows drifting apart into a list.

The white strip is the last thing on the page, so it is where a phone’s home indicator would come to rest.
Its padding grows to clear that, and to clear a display cutout beside it, on the same terms as the margin of the [Grid](/docs/components-layout-grid--docs).
The band of colour still reaches the edges of the screen; only the links move.

In print, the blue band keeps its colour rather than being flattened to save ink.

## Accessibility

A Page Footer renders a `footer` element, which is exposed as the `contentinfo` landmark.
That is what ‘How to use’ means by the footer’s landmark providing enough guidance: a heading grouping its columns would restate what the landmark already says.

The menu carries a heading that is present in the markup and hidden visually.
Screen reader users get a name for the group of links, while sighted users read the grouping from its position and its colour.
That heading is a real one, so it appears in the outline of the page and can be navigated to.

## See also

- [Page](/docs/components-containers-page--docs) – contains the Page Footer.
- [Page Header](/docs/components-containers-page-header--docs) – sits at the top of the Page.

## Design tokens

components-containers-page-header--docs.content:
{/* @license CC0-1.0 */}

import { Canvas, Controls, Description, Meta, Primary, Title } from "@storybook/addon-docs/blocks";

import { DesignTokensTable } from "#storybook/_components/DesignTokensTable/DesignTokensTable";
import tokens from "#tokens/components/ams/page-header.tokens.json";

import * as PageHeaderStories from "./PageHeader.stories.tsx";
import * as PageHeaderMenuLinkStories from "./PageHeaderMenuLink.stories.tsx";

<Meta of={PageHeaderStories} />

<Title />

<Description of={PageHeaderStories} />

<Primary />

<Controls />

## Subcomponents

The Grid Cell Narrow Window Only subcomponent accepts all Grid Cell props and is only displayed in narrow windows.
The primary example uses it to repeat a menu link below the header.

### Menu Link

Navigates to an important page.
Set `fixed` to keep the link visible next to the menu button in narrow windows, and add an `icon` to display after the text.

<Canvas of={PageHeaderMenuLinkStories.MenuLink} />

<Controls of={PageHeaderMenuLinkStories.MenuLink} />

## Usage guidelines

### When to use

All our websites must start with the Page Header.
Consistent use helps people identify, navigate, and trust our digital channels.

The Page Header is the same on every page of the website, although full-screen pages (e.g. a video or map) may hide it.

### How to use

The Page Header must show the appropriate logo and brand name.
The navigation structure can be configured freely.

#### Logo

Use the correct logo: our main one, one for a sub-brand, or the English variation.
See [Logo](/docs/components-media-logo--docs) documentation for details.

The logo links to the homepage of the site it appears on.
This is a common convention that helps people navigate back to the homepage from any page of the website.

For websites with a brand name that feature the standard Amsterdam logo, only the emblem is shown on narrow screens.

#### Brand name

The City’s main website or that of a sub-brand must not display a brand name, as the logo already includes a wordmark.

All other websites must display the name of the brand or service next to the logo.
This helps people understand they are on a different website and that its navigation is separate from the main one.

An abbreviated brand name can be shown in narrow or medium-wide windows if the full name does not fit.

#### Inline menu

The menu to the right can contain a maximum of 5 items, including the menu button.
Labels should be short to help the menu fit on a single line whenever possible.
An [icon](/docs/brand-assets-icons--docs) can be added to a menu item if it helps clarify it.
Links move into the collapsible menu on narrow windows, unless they have the `fixed` prop.

#### Menu button

The ‘Menu’ button opens the collapsible menu.
It does not appear when the Page Header has no child content.
Use `noMenuButtonOnWideWindow` to hide the menu button on wide windows when there are only a few links.

#### Collapsible menu

This menu gets accessed through the menu button and offers much room for more links.
Use the `GridCellNarrowWindowOnly` subcomponent to contain links from the inline menu that disappear in narrow windows.
Don’t add whitespace to the Grid in the collapsible menu – its container already provides this.

If the collapsible menu contains [Headings](/docs/components-text-heading--docs), give them level 2 and a size of ‘level-3’.

#### Controlling the menu

By default the Page Header keeps track of whether the collapsible menu is open.
Set `defaultOpen` to have it open on the first render.

To control the menu yourself, pass `open` and update it from the `onOpenChange` callback.
This matters most in a single-page app: the Page Header stays mounted while navigating, so the menu would otherwise stay open after someone follows a link inside it.
Keep the open state in your own component and close it whenever the route changes:

{/* prettier-ignore */}
```tsx
function Header() {
  const { pathname } = useLocation() // The current route from your router
  const [menuOpen, setMenuOpen] = useState(false)
  const [previousPathname, setPreviousPathname] = useState(pathname)

  // Close the collapsible menu whenever the route changes
  if (pathname !== previousPathname) {
    setPreviousPathname(pathname)
    setMenuOpen(false)
  }

  return (
    <PageHeader onOpenChange={setMenuOpen} open={menuOpen}>
      {/* Collapsible menu content */}
    </PageHeader>
  )
}
```

## Examples

### With moving links

Links can move from the inline menu to the collapsible one on narrow windows.
A `MenuLink` is hidden by default on narrow windows.
Use `GridCellNarrowWindowOnly` to show that same link in the collapsible menu on narrow windows.

If you do not want the `MenuLink` to be hidden, use the `fixed` prop.

In this example, ‘English’ moves to the collapsible menu, while ‘Zoeken’ does not.

<Canvas of={PageHeaderStories.WithMovingLinks} />

### Without menu button on wide windows

If you only have a few links, you may not always need a collapsible menu.
Use `noMenuButtonOnWideWindow` to hide the menu button on wide windows.
On narrow windows, the menu button will still be visible,
so do not forget to add the links to the collapsible menu.

<Canvas of={PageHeaderStories.WithoutMenuButtonOnWideWindow} />

### Without menu button

In some cases, a collapsible menu might not be necessary.
If the Page Header has no `children`, the menu button will not appear.
Remember to use the `fixed` prop if you want the inline menu links to stay in place.

<Canvas of={PageHeaderStories.WithoutMenuButton} />

### With short brand name

For brand names that may not fit in a narrow window, a shorter form can be given.
Make sure the abbreviation is widely understood.

<Canvas of={PageHeaderStories.WithShortBrandName} />

### With custom logo link

The destination and accessible text of the logo link can be customized,
as well as the logo itself and its accessible name.

<Canvas of={PageHeaderStories.WithCustomLogoLink} />

### With custom texts

The visible text of the menu button, its accessible texts and the accessible navigation description can be customized.

<Canvas of={PageHeaderStories.WithCustomTexts} />

### With custom link component

Pass a custom link component to the `logoLinkComponent` prop to use your routing library for the logo link.
Here’s an example with the Link component of Next.js:

{/* prettier-ignore */}
```tsx
import { PageHeader } from "@amsterdam/design-system-react"
import NextLink from "next/link"

const LinkComponent = (props) => <NextLink {...props} />

return <PageHeader logoLinkComponent={LinkComponent} />
```

### With different branding

Websites for the City of Amsterdam must use one of our own logos and the default menu icon.

Other organisations using this component can provide elements to display their own brand.
The image for the logo must be an svg, and its label should be ‘name of the organisation + logo’.
Set the appropriate values for the sizing tokens of [Logo](/docs/components-media-logo--docs).
A different icon for the menu button must be an svg as well.

<Canvas of={PageHeaderStories.WithDifferentBranding} />

## Design

The logo and the navigation share one area of the header rather than sitting in two columns.
The navigation holds a second, invisible copy of the logo, which reserves the space the real one occupies so the menu wraps around it at the right point.
This is what allows every link to live inside a single `nav` element while the menu still behaves as if the logo were part of the same row.

On narrow screens the standard logo is cropped to its emblem by a container 0.881 rem wide.
That figure is the midpoint between the right edge of the emblem and the left edge of the wordmark, so the crop leaves equal space on both sides and does not depend on rounding to land in the right place.

The brand name is set at the size of a level 3 Heading and balances its line lengths, so a name that wraps does not end on a single short word beside the logo.
Below the wide breakpoint a short form replaces it where one is given.

Menu links are hidden below the wide breakpoint unless they are fixed, and reappear inside the collapsible menu.
The menu button’s icon turns into a cross when the menu opens, animated only for users who have not asked for reduced motion.

The header keeps the horizontal margin of the [Grid](/docs/components-layout-grid--docs) at every breakpoint, so the logo lines up with the content below it.
It grows that margin to clear a display cutout on the same terms, which keeps the two aligned in landscape as well.

In print, the menu button keeps its blue background rather than being flattened to save ink.

## Accessibility

A Page Header renders a `header` element, which is exposed as the `banner` landmark.

The logo link is named by a sentence that is in the markup and hidden visually: ‘Ga naar de homepage’, followed by the brand name where there is one.
A link named after the picture inside it would announce as a logo rather than as a way home, which tells a screen reader user what they are looking at instead of where the link goes.

The navigation is labelled by a heading that is hidden visually and hidden from the outline as well.
It gives the `nav` landmark a name without adding a heading to the page structure, so a screen reader user hears which navigation this is when they reach it and does not meet an extra entry when they list the headings.

The menu button shows ‘Menu’ and announces something else.
Its visible word is hidden from assistive technology, and a hidden phrase in its place says whether activating it will show or hide the menu, so the name states the action rather than only the destination.
The button also reports whether the menu is open and names the region it controls.

The invisible copy of the logo inside the navigation is hidden from assistive technology and from the keyboard, so it is neither announced nor focusable a second time.

The list item holding the menu button carries the `hidden` attribute and is revealed by the stylesheet.
If that stylesheet never arrives, the collapsible menu stays visible in full instead of leaving a button that cannot open anything.

- [Page Footer](/docs/components-containers-page-footer--docs) – sits at the bottom of the Page.
- [Logo](/docs/components-media-logo--docs) – the logo shown in the Page Header.

import { Canvas, Controls, Description, Meta, Primary, Title } from "@storybook/addon-docs/blocks";

import { DesignTokensTable } from "#storybook/_components/DesignTokensTable/DesignTokensTable";
import tokens from "#tokens/components/ams/progress-list.tokens.json";

import * as ProgressListStories from "./ProgressList.stories.tsx";
import * as ProgressListStepStories from "./ProgressListStep.stories.tsx";
import * as ProgressListSubstepStories from "./ProgressListSubstep.stories.tsx";

<Meta of={ProgressListStories} />

<Title />

<Description of={ProgressListStories} />

<Primary />

<Controls />

## Subcomponents

Steps make up a Progress List.
A Step can contain Substeps, wrapped in the Substeps subcomponent, which has no props of its own.

### Step

Each step in the list has a heading, a status, and optionally collapsible content.

<Canvas of={ProgressListStepStories.Step} />

<Controls of={ProgressListStepStories.Step} />

### Substep

Marks a smaller activity within a step.
It takes a `status`, just like a Step, but has no heading.

<Canvas of={ProgressListSubstepStories.Substep} />

<Controls of={ProgressListSubstepStories.Substep} />

## Usage guidelines

### When to use

Use a Progress List to show the status of a multi-step process, such as the handling of a permit application or the phases of a construction project.

### How to use

Assign a status to each step: `completed` or `current`.
Steps without a status are considered _upcoming_.
Only one step may be `current`; all preceding steps must be `completed`.

Choose a `headingLevel` that fits the document outline.

Nesting a Substeps element inside a step does not set that step’s `hasSubsteps` prop for you: the prop is what tells the CSS to draw the connecting lines correctly.

Use on a white background only.

## Examples

### Controlled

Use `expanded` and `onToggle` on each step to let a parent component drive the expand/collapse state.
The example below keeps only one step open at a time.

<Canvas of={ProgressListStories.Controlled} />

### Collapsible

Set `collapsible` to `true` to let users expand and collapse the content of each step.
Current and upcoming steps then start expanded.
Completed ones are initially collapsed.
Use the `defaultExpanded` prop on a step to override the default behaviour.
The `onToggle` callback emits the expanded state whenever it changes.

<Canvas of={ProgressListStories.Collapsible} />

### With substeps

A step may contain a list of substeps.
They are visually subordinate to their parent step: their indicators are smaller, and they do not display a heading.

Don’t forget to set the `hasSubsteps` prop on the parent step.

<Canvas of={ProgressListStories.WithSubsteps} />

## Design

Each step is marked by a circle, with a line running between one circle and the next.
The line passes behind the circles, and each circle is ringed in the page background colour so a gap appears where the two meet.
This is why the component asks to be used on a white background only: the ring is painted, not transparent.

The line carries the progress as much as the circles do.
It is dashed and grey ahead of the current step and solid and green behind it, so the state of a step is legible from the connection as well as from the marker.

A marker is placed against the height of the heading beside it rather than against the top of the step, so the circle sits on the middle of the first line of that heading at every heading level.

Substeps repeat the same arrangement at a smaller size, and their connecting line is drawn over the parent’s so the two do not show through one another.

The last line in the list is removed rather than left hanging.

A collapsible step is opened by its own heading: the button fills the width of the heading and takes its typeface, size and weight, so the whole line is the control.
The chevron turns half a circle when the step opens, animated only for users who have not asked for reduced motion.

In print, collapsed steps are expanded again.
A printed Progress List shows the whole process rather than whatever happened to be open on screen.

## Accessibility

A Progress List renders an ordered list, so it is announced as a list with a number of items, and the steps keep their order.

The step in progress is marked as the current step, which lets assistive technology report where in the process the reader is without their having to count.

The status is conveyed visually through both colour and an icon, and via screen reader text.
You can customize the screen reader text with `completedAccessibleText` and `currentAccessibleText` (defaults: ‘Klaar’ and ‘Bezig’).
Neither the colour of a marker nor the style of a connecting line reaches a screen reader, so that text is the only thing carrying the status.

A collapsible step reports whether it is expanded and names the panel it controls.
The content of a collapsed step is removed from the page rather than hidden visually, so it is not announced and not reachable by keyboard until the step is opened.

## Design tokens

<Title />

<Description of={SpotlightStories} />

<Primary />

<Controls />

## Usage guidelines

### When not to use

Do not position a Spotlight on the [Grid](/docs/components-layout-grid--docs).

### How to use

Use the entire width of the [Page](/docs/components-containers-page--docs) container.
Wrap its content in a Grid with extra large vertical padding.

Use any of the [highlight colours](/docs/brand-design-tokens-colour--docs) for the background.
The design system does not prescribe a meaning to any of these colours.
The default is purple.

Select [the correct colour](/docs/brand-design-tokens-colour--docs#pairing-foreground-with-background-colours) for text and links against the background you choose.
On a dark background, set `color="inverse"` on every Heading, Paragraph, and Link inside the Spotlight.
On a light one, keep the default colour for headings and paragraphs, and set `color="contrast"` on links.

Name the landmark when you use the `as` prop: give the heading inside the Spotlight an `id` and point `aria-labelledby` at it.
Users of assistive technology can then tell this landmark apart from the others on the page.

Find a fitting setup for the [amount and width of columns](/docs/pages-guidelines-layout-and-spacing--docs#how-to-size-the-grid-cells).

Use the `as` prop to render a meaningful HTML element: `as="section"` for a self-contained content area, `as="aside"` for supporting content.

## Examples

### Highlight content

Use a Spotlight to direct the user’s attention to the most important or actionable content on the page.

<Canvas of={SpotlightStories.HighlightContent} />

## Design

A Spotlight is a background colour and nothing else: no padding, no border, no corner radius, and no width of its own.
It fills whatever contains it and takes its shape from the Grid inside it, which is why ‘How to use’ asks for the full width of the Page and for a Grid with extra large vertical padding.

In print, a Spotlight keeps its background colour instead of being flattened to save ink.

## Accessibility

A Spotlight carries no colour that a screen reader can report, so its emphasis is entirely visual.
Whatever the highlight is meant to signal has to be in the content itself.

The `as` prop is what gives a Spotlight a place in the structure of a page: `as="aside"` makes it a complementary landmark, and `as="section"` makes it a region once it has an accessible name.
Without a name, a `section` groups the content in the markup but adds nothing anyone can navigate to; ‘How to use’ covers how to give it one.

Which foreground colour to use depends on the highlight colour behind it, since the component sets only the background and leaves the text colour to the content inside it.

## See also

- [Page](/docs/components-containers-page--docs) – contains the Spotlight.
- [Grid](/docs/components-layout-grid--docs) – wraps the content of the Spotlight.

import { Canvas, Controls, Description, Meta, Primary, Title } from "@storybook/addon-docs/blocks";

import { DesignTokensTable } from "#storybook/_components/DesignTokensTable/DesignTokensTable";
import tokens from "#tokens/components/ams/table.tokens.json";

import * as TableStories from "./Table.stories.tsx";
import * as TableCellStories from "./TableCell.stories.tsx";
import * as TableHeaderCellStories from "./TableHeaderCell.stories.tsx";

<Meta of={TableStories} />

<Title />

<Description of={TableStories} />

<Primary />

This component has no props to configure.

## Subcomponents

A Table is composed of a Caption, a Header containing Header Cells, a Body, an optional Footer, and Rows of Cells.
Caption, Header, Body, Footer, and Row have no props of their own; the example above shows each of them in place.

### Cell

Holds a single value within a row.
Use the `align` prop to align the content to the center or end of the cell.
Apply the same value to all cells in the column and the matching `Table.HeaderCell`.

<Canvas of={TableCellStories.Cell} />

<Controls of={TableCellStories.Cell} />

### Header Cell

Labels the column of values below it.
Use the `align` prop to match the alignment of the column’s cells.

<Canvas of={TableHeaderCellStories.HeaderCell} />

<Controls of={TableHeaderCellStories.HeaderCell} />

## Usage guidelines

### How to use

Use [Margin](/docs/utilities-css-margin--docs) or [Prose](/docs/utilities-css-prose--docs) to add vertical whitespace.

Add a caption so users can find and understand the Table without reading its data.
Use a [Heading](/docs/components-text-heading--docs) in it, at the level that fits the document outline.

To place content between the Heading and the Table, keep the Caption but hide it visually, then position the heading and content above the Table.
Do not use ARIA relations; they hurt the Table's semantics (see [this article](https://www.scottohara.me/blog/2019/04/19/tabled-tables.html)).

Keep a Table narrow enough to fit where it is used.

## Examples

### With footer and row headers

Use table headers to tell users what the rows and columns represent.
Use the scope attribute to help users of assistive technology distinguish between row and column headers.
Use `Table.Footer` for a summary row.

<Canvas of={TableStories.WithFooterAndRowHeaders} />

### With heading and description

When the table needs context – a source, a date, or reading instructions – place a heading and a small paragraph above it and hide the caption visually.

<Canvas of={TableStories.WithHeadingAndDescription} />

### With caption in figure

The context can be positioned below the table as well.
In this case, use a [Figure](/docs/components-media-figure--docs) and let the Table keep its Caption.

<Canvas of={TableStories.InFigure} />

## Features

A Table wider than the space it sits in scrolls horizontally within its own container, rather than widening the page around it.
That container takes keyboard focus, so someone can scroll it with the arrow keys, not only with a pointer or touch.

## Design

Rows are separated by a single rule beneath each one.
There are no vertical lines, no zebra stripes, and no spacing between cells: the columns are held together by their alignment.

Cells align to the top of their row, so the first line of every cell in a row starts level even when one of them wraps over several lines.
Header cells in the head align to the bottom instead, which puts a column label that runs onto two lines directly above the values it names.

The caption is bold and aligned with the start of the table rather than centred over it.
It reads as the title of what follows, in the same place a heading would sit.

In print, a Table is never split across two pages.

## Accessibility

A Table caption creates the accessible name for the Table, announced by screen readers on every encounter.
That is also why ‘How to use’ warns against ARIA relations as a substitute: they name the table without giving it the caption its semantics expect.

The container that scrolls is a focusable group, which keeps the columns past its right edge reachable without a pointing device, as [WCAG 2.1.1](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#keyboard) requires.

## See also

- [Prose](/docs/utilities-css-prose--docs) – applies the recommended vertical spacing for editorial content.
- [Table Page](/docs/pages-internal-table-page--docs) – various templates for large data tables in internal websites.

<Meta of={TabsStories} />

<Title />

<Description of={TabsStories} />

<Primary />

<Controls />

## Subcomponents

The List groups the Buttons of all tabs; it has no props of its own and is visible in the example above.

### Button

Activates its tab.
Point the required `aria-controls` prop at the `id` of the corresponding Panel.

<Canvas of={TabsButtonStories.Button} />

<Controls of={TabsButtonStories.Button} />

### Panel

Holds the content of a tab.
Its `id` connects it to the Button that controls it.

<Canvas of={TabsPanelStories.Panel} />

<Controls of={TabsPanelStories.Panel} />

## Usage guidelines

### When to use

Use Tabs to let related content fragments share a space on the current page.
Each tab has a button that shows its content in a panel.

The content of each tab must be usable independent of the others.

### When not to use

Do not use Tabs to toggle between large amounts of primary content.
That would come down to navigating between pages.
In this context, use [Tab Navigation](/docs/components-navigation-tab-navigation--docs) to offer the user the benefits of links.

### How to use

Create a panel for each button.
Add an `aria-controls` attribute to each button and match its value to the `id` of the associated panel.

## Features

### Keyboard navigation

| Key            | Behaviour                                      |
| :------------- | :--------------------------------------------- |
| Enter or Space | Open or close the tab that has the focus       |
| Tab            | Go to the next element that can have focus     |
| Shift + Tab    | Go to the previous element that can have focus |
| Left arrow     | If the tabs have focus, go to the previous tab |
| Right arrow    | If the tabs have focus, go to the next tab     |
| Home           | If the tabs have focus, go to the first tab    |
| End            | If the tabs have focus, go to the last tab     |

## Design

A line runs under the whole row of tabs, and the selected tab marks itself with a thicker line of its own on top of it.
Hovering a tab that is not selected draws a line in the same colour but thinner than the selected tab’s, so a hovered tab reads as a step below the selected one rather than as a different treatment.

The selected tab is also set in bold.
A copy of the label at that bold weight sits invisibly behind every tab, reserving the width the bold text will need, so selecting a tab does not nudge its neighbours along the row.

Tabs do not shrink to fit.
When the row is too long it scrolls sideways and snaps to the start of a tab, which keeps every label readable instead of squeezing labels until they wrap or truncate.

The focus ring is drawn inside a tab rather than around it.
The row is a scrolling container, and a ring drawn outside the button would be clipped at its edge.

In forced colours mode the selected tab is filled with the system’s selection colour.
The lines that normally mark it are shadows, and shadows are not rendered in that mode.

## Accessibility

Tabs implement the tab pattern: the row is a tab list, each button is a tab that names the panel it controls and reports whether it is selected, and each panel is a tab panel labelled by its own tab.

Only the selected tab is in the tab order.
Tab therefore moves past the whole row in one step, and the arrow, Home and End keys move between the tabs, wrapping around at either end.

The panel itself can be focused, so Tab from the selected tab lands on the content it revealed rather than skipping past it.
Panels that are not selected are not rendered at all: their content is absent from the page, so it is neither announced nor found by ‘Find in page’.

The invisible bold copy of each label is hidden from assistive technology, so a tab is announced once rather than twice.

## See also

- [Tab Navigation](/docs/components-navigation-tab-navigation--docs) – when each tab should navigate to its own page.

import { Canvas, Controls, Description, Meta, Primary, Title } from "@storybook/addon-docs/blocks";

import { DesignTokensTable } from "#storybook/_components/DesignTokensTable/DesignTokensTable";
import tokens from "#tokens/components/ams/alert.tokens.json";

import * as AlertStories from "./Alert.stories.tsx";

<Meta of={AlertStories} />

<Title />

<Description of={AlertStories} />

<Primary />

<Controls />

## Usage guidelines

### When to use

Use an Alert if the message’s purpose matches one of the following:

- **Information** to bring attention to a message.
  This variation is blue and it is the default.
- **Success** to reassure that a process is complete.
  This variation is green.
- **Warning** when action is needed to prevent damage.
  This variation is orange.
- **Error** indicates an error has occurred.
  This variation is red.

### How to use

Place the Alert in a Grid Cell to create enough white space around it.

Important and urgent information is to be placed directly below the Page Header.
Examples: system outage or changes in the opening hours of a City Office.
This can be applied to the entire website or to a part of it.

Add a close button if the user should be able to dismiss the Alert.

Choose a `headingLevel` that fits the outline of the page around the Alert; there is no default.
The heading keeps the size of a level 3 Heading whichever level you pick.

You don’t need to set `headingId`: the Alert generates a unique id for its heading and labels itself with it, so several Alerts on a page never collide.
Pass one only when the heading needs a specific id of your own.

Write the heading and the text so they carry the message on their own.
The severity reaches no one through the colour or the icon alone, which is what [WCAG 1.4.1](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#use-of-color) asks you to avoid.

## Examples

### Warning

Display a warning when user action is required.

<Canvas of={AlertStories.Warning} />

### Error

In case of an error, use the red alert.
Provide the user with suggestions on alternative ways to achieve the goal.

<Canvas of={AlertStories.Error} />

### Success

Announce the success of a significant action.

<Canvas of={AlertStories.Success} />

### Information

An informative message can emphasize matters that are useful to follow.

<Canvas of={AlertStories.Info} />

### With inline link

Include an inline link in the text to guide the user.

<Canvas of={AlertStories.WithInlineLink} />

## Design

An Alert is outlined in the colour of its severity and carries a band of that same colour along its leading edge, with the icon centred in it.
The band takes its dividing line from the outline, so the two meet as one continuous stroke of the same weight.

The background behind the text stays white in all four variants.
Only the outline, the band and the icon change colour, which keeps the text on the same background as the rest of the page and its contrast the same whatever the severity.

The heading is fixed at the size of a level 3 Heading, independent of the `headingLevel` given to it.
Two Alerts then look alike wherever they sit in the outline of a page.

In print, the band keeps its colour rather than being flattened to save ink.
It is the only part told to do so, because without it nothing distinguishes one severity from another on paper.

## Accessibility

An Alert renders a `section` labelled by its heading, which makes it a `region` landmark.
Assistive technology lists it with the other landmarks, so users can reach the message directly instead of hunting for it.

The label is wired up with `aria-labelledby` rather than left to the heading inside.
NVDA in Chrome does not read that heading as the name of the section otherwise.
Setting `headingId` to `null` removes the label, and the landmark with it.

An Alert does not announce itself when it appears.
It is not a live region, so it suits a message that is already there when a view renders rather than one that must interrupt.

The icon carries no text alternative and the severity is conveyed by colour alone, so neither reaches a screen reader.
Both are reinforcement for a message the heading and text already carry, as described under ‘How to use’.

import { Canvas, Controls, Description, Meta, Primary, Title } from "@storybook/addon-docs/blocks";

import { DesignTokensTable } from "#storybook/_components/DesignTokensTable/DesignTokensTable";
import tokens from "#tokens/components/ams/avatar.tokens.json";

import * as AvatarStories from "./Avatar.stories.tsx";

<Meta of={AvatarStories} />

<Title />

<Description of={AvatarStories} />

<Primary />

<Controls />

## Usage guidelines

### When to use

Show an Avatar for the user of the website, or to associate a person with a content item.

### How to use

On a page in another language, set `initialsAccessibleName` and `userAccessibleName` so the Avatar is announced in that language rather than in Dutch.
Each replaces the entire announcement and is used verbatim, so repeat the initials in `initialsAccessibleName` when they should still be spoken.

## Examples

### With image

The Avatar can also display a photo or other image for the person.
Make sure to scale the image down to around 100 pixels to prevent unnecessary data transfers.
The center of the image will be visible; provide a square image if possible.

<Canvas of={AvatarStories.WithImage} />

### Fallback icon

A user icon displays if no label and image are provided.

<Canvas of={AvatarStories.FallbackIcon} />

## Design

The Avatar contains 1 or 2 initial letters from the person’s full name, a picture, or a generic icon.
The component takes the first two characters of the label and sets them in capitals, so the shape stays the same however the name was written.

To personalize the Avatar, the user can be allowed to choose one of the [highlight colours](/docs/brand-design-tokens-colour--docs).
The default is purple.
The design system does not define a meaning to any of these background colours.

The circle is sized from the text it holds rather than from a fixed measurement: its width follows the font size and line height of the initials.
An Avatar showing an image drops the border and grows by exactly the space that border and its padding occupied, so both kinds line up at the same size beside each other.

An image is cropped to the circle from its centre and scaled to cover it, whatever proportions it arrives in.
A portrait that is not square therefore loses its edges rather than distorting.

In print, an Avatar keeps its background colour instead of being flattened to save ink.

## Accessibility

An Avatar is announced exactly once, through a line of text that is in the markup but hidden visually.
The initials themselves are marked `aria-hidden`, and an image is given an empty `alt`.

That hidden text defaults to Dutch: ‘Initialen gebruiker’ followed by the initials, or ‘Gebruiker’ when the label is empty.
It is built from the label even when an image is displayed, so an Avatar showing a photograph is still announced by its initials.
Neither wording is fixed: both can be configured, so an Avatar can be announced in the language of the page it sits on.

import { Canvas, Controls, Description, Meta, Primary, Title } from "@storybook/addon-docs/blocks";

import * as BadgeStories from "./Badge.stories.tsx";

<Meta of={BadgeStories} />

<Title />

<Description of={BadgeStories} />

<Primary />

<Controls />

## Usage guidelines

### How to write

Let the Badge contain a short text or a number.

Write a label that stands on its own without the colour behind it.
Nothing but the label reaches a screen reader, and a colour is not a message anyone should have to read, which is what [WCAG 1.4.1](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#use-of-color) asks of you.

## Examples

### With icon

Include an icon when it provides meaning that isn’t obvious from the text alone, or when it helps with quick recognition.
This may be helpful for statuses, alerts, or categories that users look over instead of reading.

<Canvas of={BadgeStories.WithIcon} />

## Design

Use any of the feedback or highlight [colours](/docs/brand-design-tokens-colour--docs) for the background.
The default is green.
Red, orange and green are especially useful for showing an error, warning, or success.
However, they can also be combined with the other colours without carrying these meanings.

A Badge is set in bold at the size and line height of body text, and it is padded on the left and right but not above and below.
Its coloured block is therefore exactly as tall as one line of text, so a Badge placed in a sentence or a table cell does not push the lines around it apart.

The corners are square and there is no border.
The colour fills the block, which is what makes a Badge read as a label applied to something rather than as a control to press.

In print, a Badge keeps its background colour instead of being flattened to save ink.

## Accessibility

A Badge renders a `span` with no role of its own, so its text is read as part of the sentence or the cell it sits in rather than announced separately.

Neither the background colour nor an icon reaches a screen reader; the label carries the whole message on its own.
‘How to write’ covers what that asks of the wording.

components-feedback-skeleton--docs.title: Components/Feedback/Skeleton
components-feedback-skeleton--docs.content: {/* @license CC0-1.0 */} import { Canvas, Controls, Description, Meta, Primary, Title } from "@storybook/addon-docs/blocks"; import { DesignTokensTable } from "#storybook/_components/DesignTokensTable/DesignTokensTable"; import tokens from "#tokens/components/ams/skeleton.tokens.json"; import * as SkeletonStories from "./Skeleton.stories.tsx"; import * as SkeletonHeadingStories from "./SkeletonHeading.stories.tsx"; import * as SkeletonImageStories from "./SkeletonImage.stories.tsx"; import * as SkeletonListStories from "./SkeletonList.stories.tsx"; import * as SkeletonParagraphStories from "./SkeletonParagraph.stories.tsx"; import * as SkeletonTableStories from "./SkeletonTable.stories.tsx"; <Description of={SkeletonStories} /> <Primary /> <Controls /> The Skeleton container takes only the parts you compose inside it and hides them from assistive technologies. Each part has its own options, documented under Subcomponents. The container itself has no props to configure; the controls above set the props of the parts in this example. ## Subcomponents Compose a Skeleton from its parts: Skeleton.Image, Skeleton.Heading, Skeleton.Paragraph, Skeleton.List, and Skeleton.Table. Skeleton.Image is a single block; the others render one or more lines, sized to the text they stand in for. Set the `lines`, `rows`, and `columns` props to approximate the amount of content you expect. ### Heading Lines the size of a Heading. Set `lines` above one for a heading that wraps onto several lines. <Canvas of={SkeletonHeadingStories.Heading} /> <Controls of={SkeletonHeadingStories.Heading} /> ### Paragraph Lines the size of body text. Their lengths alternate between two widths, and the last line of a multi-line paragraph is shorter, approximating its ragged end. <Canvas of={SkeletonParagraphStories.Paragraph} /> <Controls of={SkeletonParagraphStories.Paragraph} /> ### List Body-text lines, each with a marker, indented like an Unordered List. <Canvas of={SkeletonListStories.List} /> <Controls of={SkeletonListStories.List} /> ### Table A grid of cells. <Canvas of={SkeletonTableStories.Table} /> <Controls of={SkeletonTableStories.Table} /> ### Image A block that stands in for an image. Set the `aspectRatio` prop to match the image that will replace it; it defaults to 16:9. <Canvas of={SkeletonImageStories.Image} /> <Controls of={SkeletonImageStories.Image} /> ## Usage guidelines ### When to use Show a Skeleton while loading content that takes a noticeable time to arrive – roughly between 1 and 10 seconds. Compose the parts to mirror the content to come, so the grey blocks prepare users for the page structure and waiting feels shorter. ### When not to use Do not show a Skeleton for waits shorter than about a second: a flash of grey blocks is more distracting than helpful. For a process with a known duration or progress, such as a file upload, show actual progress information instead. Never use a Skeleton for content that is already available – render that content immediately. Avoid combining it with other loading indicators in the same view. ### How to use Nest the parts you need inside a Skeleton, in the order the real content will appear. Match the number of lines, rows, and columns to the expected content, so replacing the Skeleton barely shifts the layout. Render a Skeleton only while its content is loading, and replace it with the content – or an empty or error state – as soon as that content arrives. A Skeleton is decorative and hidden from assistive technologies, so it stays silent on its own. Announcing the loading state is the job of the region that holds the content, not of each Skeleton – otherwise a list of ten Skeletons would announce ten times. Mark that region with `aria-busy` while it loads, and give it a single, always-present status message whose text changes from a loading message to the result: ```html <section aria-busy="true"> <p class="ams-visually-hidden" role="status">Zoekresultaten worden geladen</p> <!-- ten Skeletons while loading --> </section> ``` When the content has loaded, replace the Skeletons with it, set `aria-busy` to `false`, and change the status message – for example to ‘10 resultaten gevonden’. A Loading Region component that wraps this pattern is planned. #### Customising the animation The animation is set through one custom property, `--ams-skeleton-animation`, which holds a CSS `animation` shorthand. Override it to suit your theme: change the duration or timing function to adjust the pace, point it at your own `@keyframes` to replace the motion, or set it to `none` to switch it off. Users who prefer reduced motion never see the animation, whatever you set it to. ## Features The dimensions of the lines derive from the design tokens of the text they mimic: Skeleton.Heading follows Heading 2, and the other parts follow body text. Each line is exactly as tall as its line of text, so a part occupies the same height as the content it stands in for and the layout barely shifts once that content arrives. Line lengths vary deterministically: within each part the lines – or, in a table, the cells across each row – alternate between two widths, and any part with more than one ends on a shorter last one. This looks natural yet renders identically on every request, which keeps server-side rendering consistent and visual regression tests stable. ## Design The blocks use a single neutral grey that reads as a quiet backdrop rather than content. The space between composed parts is a generic gap rather than the exact margins of any one component, keeping the Skeleton reusable in any layout. A calm heartbeat signals that loading is under way. Two quick beats in succession – the second softer than the first – fade the blocks to a lighter shade and back, then a longer rest holds them at full strength before the next pair. The rhythm reassures without demanding attention, closer to a resting heartbeat than a busy shimmer. It sits behind a single design token, so a theme can retime it, point it at its own keyframes, or switch it off. ## Accessibility A Skeleton renders with `aria-hidden="true"`, so screen readers skip the grey blocks entirely. Because the loading announcement belongs to the region that is loading rather than to each block, the Skeleton stays silent; the application announces the state once for the region, as shown under ‘How to use’, to meet [WCAG 4.1.3](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#status-messages). Setting `aria-busy="true"` on that region also permits assistive technology to hold back updates to the status message inside it and deliver them as one update once it turns false. The ARIA spec allows this rather than requiring it, so not every screen reader does. A Loading Region component to encapsulate that pattern is planned. The animation runs only for users who have not asked for reduced motion; everyone else sees the static blocks. In forced colours mode, the blocks remain visible through the system colour for disabled text. ## See also - [Card](/docs/components-navigation-card--docs), [Paragraph](/docs/components-text-paragraph--docs), [Heading](/docs/components-text-heading--docs), [Ordered List](/docs/components-text-ordered-list--docs), [Unordered List](/docs/components-text-unordered-list--docs), [Image](/docs/components-media-image--docs) and [Table](/docs/components-containers-table--docs) – the components a Skeleton can stand in for. ## Design tokens <DesignTokensTable tokens={tokens} />

<Meta of={CharacterCountStories} />

<Title />

<Description of={CharacterCountStories} />

<Primary />

<Controls />

## Usage guidelines

### When to use

Only use a Character Count when there is a good reason for limiting the number of characters users can enter.
For example, if there is an indication that users are likely to enter more information than they need to.
Or when there is a legal or technical reason that means an entry must be no more than a certain number of characters.

### When not to use

If your users keep hitting the character limit imposed by the backend of your service then try to increase the limit rather than use a Character Count.

## Examples

### Error

When the length exceeds the maximum length, the colour of the text changes to red.

<Canvas of={CharacterCountStories.Error} />

### Translated text

The component displays its text in Dutch by default.
Pass one of the exported formatters – or a custom function – to `formatText` to display the count in another language.
The Arabic formatter applies Arabic number–noun agreement.
See the [Localisation developer guide](/docs/docs-developer-guide-localisation--docs) for the tested locales.

<Canvas of={CharacterCountStories.Translated} />

## Features

Users will get updates at a pace that works best for the way they interact with the textarea.
This means:

- sighted users will see a count message that updates as they type;
- screen reader users will hear the count announcement when they stop typing.

This component does not restrict the user from entering information.
The user can enter more than the character limit, but are told they’ve entered too many characters.
This lets them type or copy and paste their full answer, then edit it down.

## Design

A Character Count is one line of small text below the field.
It keeps the ordinary text colour instead of being greyed down, so a reader who needs to check the count is not asked to read weaker text than the rest of the form.

Going over the limit turns it red, and that is the whole of the change: no icon, no border, and nothing about the field itself.

Counting up towards the limit rather than down from it means the message says the same thing before and after the limit is passed.
The wording never has to switch from characters remaining to characters too many.

## Accessibility

A Character Count is a status region, so screen readers announce the new count without moving focus and without interrupting what is being read.
Someone typing hears the count between words rather than after every keystroke, which is what ‘Features’ above describes.

The text is fixed Dutch — the count, the word ‘van’, the limit, and ‘tekens’ — and cannot be configured.
That is worth weighing before using a Character Count on a page in another language.

Going over the limit is signalled by colour alone, so the count itself has to be read for the change to register.
The text says the same thing either way, which is what keeps the message complete without the colour.
